handbookNote: Wisconsin Commercial Driver's Manual (May 2026 edition), published by the Wisconsin Department of Transportation (WisDOT) Division of Motor Vehicles -- fetched directly from the official WisDOT-hosted PDF at https://wisconsindot.gov/Documents/dmv/shared/bds356-cdl-manual.pdf on 2026-08-24 (5.72MB PDF, full text extracted via pdftotext -layout to scratchpad/wi_cdl_research/wi_cdl_manual_full.txt, 11,035 lines, cross-checked against a pdftotext -raw extraction for column-misaligned tables), supplemented by the official WisDOT CDL manual landing page at https://wisconsindot.gov/Pages/dmv/com-drv-vehs/cdl-how-aply/cdl-manual.aspx (checked 2026-08-24). Price matches this project's established CDL tier ($6.99). Real exam mechanics are HEDGED: an exhaustive keyword search of the full extracted manual text (for 'questions', '%', 'percent', 'passing score', 'correctly to pass', 'number of items', and similar terms) found that Wisconsin's own manual describes WHICH knowledge tests exist (Section 1.1.1: General Knowledge Test taken by all applicants, plus separate Passenger Transport, Air Brakes, Combination Vehicles, Hazardous Materials, Tank Vehicle, Doubles/Triples, and School Bus tests as applicable) and WHICH three-part skills test sequence applies (vehicle inspection, basic vehicle control, on-road driving, taken in that order per Section 1.1.2), but at no point states an item count per knowledge test or a numeric/percentage passing score for the knowledge tests -- confirmed by exhaustive search, this figure simply does not appear anywhere in the fetched official text. The WisDOT CDL manual landing page likewise does not state these figures. The one official Wisconsin DMV document found to state an explicit 80% passing score is the WisDOT CDL Instructor Guidelines (https://wisconsindot.gov/Documents/dmv/shared/cdl-instructor-guidelines.pdf, fetched 2026-08-24), but that 80% figure is for the driving-instructor licensing knowledge test (WI Stat 343.62(4)(a)1), NOT the CDL applicant knowledge test itself, so it is cited here only as corroborating context, not as a confirmed CDL-applicant figure. The federally standardized 80% minimum passing score for CDL knowledge tests under 49 CFR 383.135(a) applies regardless and is the de facto floor every state's CDL program must meet; third-party CDL test-prep aggregators (not used as a source for any question content) converge on a General Knowledge test of 50 questions with 40 correct needed to pass, consistent with the AAMVA base-manual convention seen in several other CDL-track states in this project, but this specific item count could not be confirmed on any wisconsindot.gov or wisconsindmv.gov source and is therefore NOT asserted as fact anywhere in this question bank -- per this project's no-default-values discipline, it is explicitly hedged rather than borrowed from another state or an unverified third party. What IS confirmed directly from the official Wisconsin manual: Wisconsin's CDL vehicle classes are A (combination vehicle, GCWR over 26,000 lbs with a towed unit GVWR over 10,000 lbs), B (heavy straight vehicle, GVWR over 26,000 lbs), and C (small vehicle under 26,001 lbs GVWR that is either designed for 16+ passengers including the driver or hauls placardable hazardous materials), with a flowchart in the front matter walking through class determination; Wisconsin's CDL endorsements are S (School Bus), P (Passenger, 16+ including driver), H (Hazardous Materials), N (Tank Vehicles), T (Double/Triple Trailers), and F (Farm Service, restricted to farm service operation) -- notably Wisconsin uses a distinct 'F' Farm Service endorsement rather than the combined Tank/Hazmat 'X' endorsement seen in several other CDL-track states in this project; Wisconsin's CDL restriction codes are K (intrastate only), 51 (intrastate only in excepted industry), V (CMV medical variance required), L (no air-brake-equipped CMV), Z (no full-air-brake-equipped CMV, skills test taken in partial-air-brake vehicle), E (no manual-transmission CMV), O (no tractor/trailer CMV), M (no Class A passenger vehicle), N (no Class A/B passenger vehicle), and X (no cargo in CMV tank vehicle) -- note Wisconsin reuses 'N' and 'X' as both an endorsement letter and, in different contexts, a restriction code, a genuine Wisconsin-specific quirk preserved rather than smoothed over. A Commercial Learner Permit (CLP) is valid for 180 days and must be held at least 14 days before a skills test may be attempted (also required to lift restrictions Z, E, O, N or add an S/P endorsement); only P, S, and N endorsements may be added to a CLP. The three skills-test segments (vehicle inspection, basic vehicle control, on-road driving) must all be passed on the same CLP and taken in that order, administered by DMV-authorized third-party examiners with a minimum two-day waiting period to schedule. The 'H' Hazardous Materials endorsement requires an FBI fingerprint-based criminal background check and TSA threat assessment, proof of U.S. citizenship or legal status, is valid up to five years on first issuance (coordinated with CDL expiration) and four years on each renewal thereafter, with fingerprinting/background checks repeated at first renewal and every four years after. The 'S' School Bus endorsement requires knowledge, road-signs, vision, and skills tests, a background check (self-certified on form MV3740, re-run at each renewal and every 4 years), and a medical exam every 2 years (annually if 70+); renewal requires the knowledge test, signs test, vision, and an abbreviated skills test. Section 1.3 (CDL Disqualifications) in Wisconsin's own manual does not enumerate specific disqualification durations in the text itself -- it explicitly defers to an online list ('See list of CDL disqualifications online... search "CDL disqualifications"'), so this question bank does not assert Wisconsin-specific disqualification-duration figures that the manual itself withholds; Section 1.4 (Other CDL rules) does give concrete figures used here, including: driving without a CDL or holding more than one license can draw a fine up to $5,000 or jail time; drivers must notify their employer within 30 days of any traffic-violation conviction (except parking) and within 2 business days of a suspension/revocation/disqualification; hazmat endorsement holders must surrender their 'H' endorsement within 24 hours of a disqualifying conviction or indictment. Content-depth rationale: Wisconsin's manual is organized into Part One (Section 1 Introduction), Section 2 Driving Safely (by far the largest section -- split here into two buckets: 02_driving_safely_a covering 2.1 Vehicle inspection through 2.16 Mountain driving, 03_driving_safely_b covering 2.17 Driving emergencies through 2.23 Hazardous materials rules for all commercial drivers), Part Two (Section 3 Transporting Cargo Safely, Section 4 Transporting Passengers Safely, Section 5 Air Brakes, Section 6 Combination Vehicles, Section 7 Doubles and Triples, Section 8 Tank Vehicles, Section 9 Hazardous Materials -- the second-largest section, split here into two buckets: 10_hazmat_a covering 9.1-9.4, 11_hazmat_b covering 9.5-9.8 including the hazmat glossary, Section 10 School Buses -- a substantial, Wisconsin-detailed section covering danger zones/mirror use, loading/unloading, emergency exit/evacuation, railroad crossings, student management, ABS, and special safety considerations), and Part Three (Section 11M Vehicle Inspection Test, Section 12M Basic Control Skills Test, Section 13 On-Road Driving Test -- the latter two combined into one bucket given their comparatively short combined length), plus Wisconsin-specific administrative front matter (Entry Level Driver Training requirements, CDL classes/endorsements/restrictions, CLP rules, school bus and hazmat endorsement detail, farm service CDL, medical requirements) layered into the licensing bucket. Some sections (Cargo, Tank Vehicles, Doubles/Triples) are naturally short in Wisconsin's manual and their question buckets were sized down accordingly rather than padded to match larger sections. Every question in this bank is grounded in a specific passage of the fetched official Wisconsin manual text cited in that question's source_note; none are invented, generic, or borrowed from another state's numbers -- all numeric specifications (air brake PSI thresholds, following-distance/stopping-distance figures, weight thresholds, endorsement/restriction codes, permit validity periods) were verified against the actual Wisconsin text read by the drafting process, not assumed from other states' manuals even where those states share the same general AAMVA-style CDL manual structure.
